title: The New Science of Plant Intelligence and the Mystery of What Makes a Mind
content:
[![Image 1: The New Science of Plant Intelligence and the Mystery of What Makes a Mind](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/thelighteaters.jpg?fit=320%2C486&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Light-Eaters-Unseen-Intelligence-Understanding/dp/0063073854/?tag=braipick-20)

“A leaf of grass is no less than the journey work of the stars,” Walt Whitman [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/12/17/sarah-kay-astronaut-whitman/) a decade before Darwin gasped at how incomprehensible “the marvelous complexity” of organic beings is, insisting that “each living creature must be looked at as a microcosm — a little universe, formed of a host of self-propagating organisms, inconceivably minute and as numerous as the stars in heaven.”

And yet this view does not come naturally to us humans, sensemaking creatures compelled to order the universe into comprehensible categories and value ranks, compelled to rank ourselves at the top. Even Darwin had to continually calibrate that impulse. “Never say higher or lower,” he exhorted himself in his marginalia on a book he was reading while working out his evolutionary theory. “Say more complicated.”

The crux of our difficulty is both profound and banal — to understand nature through degrees of complexity rather than levels of hierarchy scaffolded with self-reference is to find ourselves no longer the pinnacle of creation. We are only just beginning to [comprehending non-human minds](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/12/14/the-soul-of-an-octopus-sy-montgomery/), only just beginning to concede that there are infinitely many [other ways of seeing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/12/24/owls-auditory-map/) and [other ways of being](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/05/09/baker-peregrine/) within the same reality; we would [sooner grant consciousness to AI](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/03/02/god-human-animal-machine/), modeled on our own minds arising from nervous systems crowned with brains, than consider different forms of intelligence as portals to a wider conception of consciousness.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/thetempleofflora_DragonArum.jpg?resize=680%2C876&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/dragon-arum-arum-dracunculus-from-the-temple-of-flora-1812-benefitting-the-nature-conservancy_framed-print?curator=brainpicker)

Dragon arum (_Arum dracunculus_) from [_The Temple of Flora_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/11/07/the-temple-of-flora-thornton/), 1812. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/dragon-arum-arum-dracunculus-from-the-temple-of-flora-1812-benefitting-the-nature-conservancy_framed-print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/cards?sort=new?curator=brainpicker), benefitting The Nature Conservancy.)

In [**_The Light Eaters: How the Unseen World of Plant Intelligence Offers a New Understanding of Life on Earth_**](https://www.amazon.com/Light-Eaters-Unseen-Intelligence-Understanding/dp/0063073854/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1421933387)), journalist Zoë Schlanger offers a mighty antidote to our tyranny of self-reference through the emerging science of organic beings we have long treated as stage decor for the drama of our earthly lives — a science rife with controversy and confusion, which is always the mark of a paradigm breaking down and breaking open, contouring a new way of thinking about questions of consciousness, communication, memory, gender, personality, interdependence, and agency. Rising from the pages is that rare achievement of meeting otherness on its own terms while broadening and deepening the terms on which we live our human lives. Schlanger draws from the world of plants “a masterclass in living to one’s fullest, weirdest, most resourceful potential,” and a counterpoint to the survival-of-the-fittest model of the natural world, intimating instead that the animating force of life may be not a combat for a kill but “an improvisation, or a collaboration, or something else entirely.”

A quarter millennium after Darwin’s grandfather [popularized the young science of botany through poetry](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/12/24/owls-auditory-map/), and two centuries after Emily Dickinson wrote that [“to be a Flower is profound Responsibility,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/04/universe-in-verse-bloom/) Schlanger writes:

> A life spent constantly growing yet rooted in a single spot comes with tremendous challenges. To meet them, plants have come up with some of the most creative methods for surviving of any living thing, us included. Many are so ingenious that they seem nearly impossible for an order of life we’ve mostly relegated to the margins of our own lives, the decoration that frames the theatrics of being an animal. Yet there they are all the same, these unbelievable abilities of plants, defying our anemic expectations. Their way of life is so astonishing, I will soon learn, that no one yet really knows the limits of what a plant can do. In fact, it seemed that no one quite knows what a plant really is.

This perplexity, Schlanger observes, is one of the most exciting things to happen in our lifetime — “depending on how comfortable you feel with seismic shifts in what you once thought to be true.” Looking back on the past half-century of botany, she reflects on this generative discomfort:

> Controversy in a scientific field tends to be a harbinger of something new, some new understanding of its subject… The more botanists uncovered the complexity of forms and behaviors of plants, the less the traditional assumptions about plant life seemed to apply.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/thetempleofflora_auriculas-1.jpg?resize=680%2C908&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/auriculas-from-the-temple-of-flora-1812-benefitting-the-nature-conservancy_framed-print?curator=brainpicker)

Auriculas from [_The Temple of Flora_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/11/07/the-temple-of-flora-thornton/), 1812. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/auriculas-from-the-temple-of-flora-1812-benefitting-the-nature-conservancy_framed-print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/cards?sort=new?curator=brainpicker), benefitting The Nature Conservancy.)

One of those assumptions stems from our basic taxonomic model of life on Earth, separated into six kingdoms — as though plants, animals, fungi, and all the rest are separate and sovereign territories of being, bound by borders and occasionally at war for resources. This tendency to mistake our models of reality for reality itself, universal to the human animal and manifested across all cultures in different ways, and this particular blind spot of Western science, unshared by indigenous and Eastern traditions, have left our view of plants on par with Descartes’s view of non-human animals. An epoch after the poetic naturalist John Muir observed that [“when we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/05/10/john-muir-nature-writings/) Schlanger writes:

> For us to truly be part of this world, to be awake to its roiling aliveness, we need to understand plants. They suffuse our atmosphere with the oxygen we breathe, and they quite literally build our bodies out of sugars they spin from sunlight. They made the ingredients that first allowed our lives to blink into existence at all. Yet they are not merely utilitarian supply machines. They have complex, dynamic lives of their own.

Out of those lives arose an organizing principle for life on Earth. In a passage that contours the central question of the entire field of plant intelligence — how something without a brain can respond to its conditions in coordinated, adaptive ways that optimize its future — Schlanger writes:

> When plants climbed out of the ocean some five hundred million years ago, they arrived in a terrestrial barrens enveloped in an inhospitable fog of carbon dioxide and hydrogen. Inhospitable, that is, to everything but plants. They had already learned to unlock oxygen from the carbon dioxide dissolved in the ocean. They adapted the technology to their new world. In a way, they brought the ocean up with them. By incessantly breathing out, those legions of early land plants tipped the balance of gases toward oxygenation. They created the atmosphere we now enjoy. It’s not a stretch to say they birthed the habitable world.

We know this — we know that [without the evolution of flowers, we wouldn’t exist](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/04/universe-in-verse-bloom/); we know that chlorophyll is [the crowning molecular miracle of nature](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/26/why-leaves-change-color/), the only thing we know that can convert the inanimate elements of air and light into sugar, that lifeblood of the living world. With an eye to our own embodiment as cathedrals of glucose, Schlanger puts this alchemy in sobering perspective:

> We are made of glucose, too. Without a constant supply of the plant sugar, our vital functions would quickly cease. Think about it: every animal organ was built with sugar from plants. The meat of our bones and indeed the bones themselves carry the signature of their molecules. Our bodies are fabricated with the threads of material plants first spun. Likewise, every thought that has ever passed through your brain was made possible by plants.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/emilydickinson_herbarium8.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/23/emily-dickinson-herbarium/)

Page from [Emily Dickinson’s herbarium](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/23/emily-dickinson-herbarium/)

Drawing on her personal obsession with plants — a portal of wonder and optimism she discovered while suffering the psychic toll of working as a climate journalist — Schlanger seeks out the pioneers of this changing paradigm. She meets a rare-plant botanist on the brink of seventy who climbs down immense volcanic cliffs to save endangered species and self-medicates for the grief of extinction by writing poetry; she chronicles the research that led to the first clear evidence of mechanosensitive ion channels in plants — those rudiments of nervous systems, enabling organisms to experience touch at the cellular level — sparked by botanist Barbara Pickard’s groundbreaking work on plant electricity; she visits with scientists who study the most controversial frontlines of plant intelligence — research that unsteadies our grip on concepts we consider singularly human.

One botanist who studies how sagebrush send distress signals to each other has found that individual plants appear to have different risk tolerance — a metric of personality, the very notion of which in an organism without a brain-based mind challenges our central assumptions about consciousness. Other research on a family of flowering desert shrubs found that female plants heed signals from both male and female plants, but males only heed other males — intimations of preference and judgment, also features of personality and consciousness. Schlanger synthesizes some of the most provocative findings:

> Plants could be said to have dialects, and are alert to their contexts enough to know when to deploy them. More than that, they have a clear sense of who is who; who is family, and who is not. They are in touch with their surroundings, and with the fluctuating status of their enemies. Their communication is not just rudimentary but complex and layered, alive with multiple meanings.

In fact, no aspect of this new botany is more paradigm-shifting than the study of plant communication. (Canadian forester Suzanne Simard’s epoch-making research into [mycorrhizal tree communication](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/07/10/trees-ted-ed/) was the fulcrum that began shifting the paradigm.) Schlanger considers how this very notion changes our understanding of nature:

> Communication implies a recognition of self and what lies beyond it — the existence of other selves. Communication is the forming of threads between individuals. It’s a way to make one life useful to other lives, to make oneself important to other selves. It turns individuals into a community. If it is true that a whole forest or field is in communication, it changes the nature of that forest or field. It changes the notion of what a plant is.

It also changes the notion of what a mind is. We have taken it to be the product of a brain attached to a nervous system, but perhaps a mind is a complex, self-organizing system networked across the entire organism. Perhaps the whole plant is a mind.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/OfraAmit_UniverseInVerse_cover_white.jpg?resize=680%2C661&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/05/01/the-universe-in-verse-book/)

Art by Ofra Amit for [_The Universe in Verse_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/05/01/the-universe-in-verse-book/)

Emerging from this particular field of science is a larger lens on the nature of knowledge. A century and a half after astronomer Maria Mitchell [contemplated the fate of science](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/08/01/maria-mitchell-diaries/), observing that “we reach forth and strain every nerve, but we seize only a bit of the curtain that hides the infinite from us,” Schlanger writes:

> The world is a prism, not a window. Wherever we look, we find new refractions.

Couple [**_The Light Eaters_**](https://www.amazon.com/Light-Eaters-Unseen-Intelligence-Understanding/dp/0063073854/?tag=braipick-20) with [the poetic science of the ghost pipe](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/08/23/ghost-pipe/) — Earth’s most supernatural plant, which thrives mysteriously without eating light — then revisit this triptych meditation on [flowers and the meaning of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/20/michael-pollan-flowers-botany-of-desire/).

title: The Gen Z Revolt Sweeping South Asia
content:
Credits

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

OSLO, Norway — Generational discontent carries within it the seeds of the future. While its eruptions herald change, the changes it brings can take many forms.

The cultural consequences of the youth revolt that shook the West in the 1960s only became apparent decades later as the long march of its values coursed through all social norms and institutions. What the wired Gen Z revolt that is today spreading across the “global South” from Bangladesh to Nepal to India and elsewhere will ultimately bring is yet to be fully known. Movements from Kenya to Madagascar, inspired by their South Asian counterparts, are closely following events online and learning best practices.

The common cause of the widespread upheaval is corruption and a lack of accountability among often nominally democratic authorities, cojoining with a howling absence of opportunity for educated youth to find gainful employment and a path toward upward mobility.

As these movements gain momentum, governments have inevitably attempted to cut off the viral storm by shutting down social media and deploying police crackdowns, only further fueling the fury and catapulting a rebellion against specific conditions into a full-blown systemic challenge.

The Monsoon Revolution in Bangladesh in the summer of 2024, led by university students in a nation where half the population is under 30, toppled the repressive government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina after a brutal crackdown on demonstrations against a quota system for government jobs.

Following her ouster, an interim government was formed, led by Nobel Peace laureate and pioneer of micro-credit for the poor, Muhammad Yunus. In July, the first contested election in three decades was held along with a referendum on a proposed constitutional charter. That brought the Bangladeshi Nationalist Party/Jamaat-e-Islami alliance to power and a vote in favor of the charter. With differences now between the ruling coalition and the constitutional charter, the future of reform is uncertain.

In September 2025, the “Gen Z” revolution in Nepal started as a viral campaign against the corruption and nepotism of high-living elites in an impoverished nation where nearly 60% of the population is under 30. After the government tried to curb connectivity by cracking down on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and YouTube, the movement predictably exploded. As in Bangladesh, protests over specific conditions morphed into a comprehensive challenge to the system.

Nepal’s Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli was forced to resign. A brief interim government headed by a former chief justice was formed until new parliamentary elections were held. In those elections, the newly formed Rastriya Swatantra Party won a majority and the 36-year-old popular rapper and former mayor of Kathmandu, Balendra Shah, was named prime minister.

The new government is still struggling to address economic stagnation, high youth unemployment and constitutional reform. Moreover, Gen Z’s governing aspirations face new challenges beyond the limited capacity of their small country.

The most moving presentation at a gathering of Nobel Peace Prize laureates and Gen Z activists I recently attended in Oslo to discuss “democracy on the brink” was from 26-year-old Rakshya Bam, a leader of the Nepalese revolution.

Offering tearful condolences to the many thousands of her fellow citizens swept away in the tsunami-scale flood unleashed by a melting glacier that collapsed at the China-Nepal border, she pleaded for the world to understand that climate change doesn’t stop at national boundaries.

The horrifying tragedy, Bam said, made her realize that the quest for justice in the world Gen Z is growing up in cannot be realized unless the local is linked to the planetary. There can be no talk of justice in any society unless [the](http://www.noemamag.com/the-gen-z-revolt-sweeping-south-asia)ongoing climate calamity is addressed. And that is the responsibility not of any one nation or government, but of all civil society, and across all borders.

Gen Z attention has now turned to India. There, the youth movement that coalesced into what became known as the Cockroach Janta Party, which garnered 22 million followers online virtually overnight, started with a protest against the Education Ministry’s cancellation of entry exams for medical schools. With incisive humor, the movement appropriated the “cockroach” name from [an insult](https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/22/india/india-cockroach-janta-party-gen-z-intl-hnk) by India’s chief justice, who said, _“There are youngsters like cockroaches, they don’t get any employment, they don’t have any place in a profession.”_

Half of India’s population — around 700 million people — are under the age of 30.

As always, a crackdown on demonstrations escalated everything.

> “Generational discontent carries within it the seeds of the future.”

In a humiliation for India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who projects the image of a strongman in control, his education minister was forced to resign to quell the unrest.

Modi’s India is unlikely to succumb to the Gen Z upsurge like in the weaker states of Bangladesh and Nepal. Nonetheless, protests over the narrow issue of medical school exams have now taken on the cast of a systemic challenge to a lack of opportunity for young people in the world’s largest country, where the GDP grew 7.8% in 2025. Stay tuned.

As Shashi Tharoor, a celebrated author, opposition member of the Indian Parliament and former under-secretary-general of the United Nations, put it: “Gen Z is transforming South Asia. Facing diminished economic prospects, many young people see not flawed institutions in need of gradual reform, but predatory systems robbing them of their future. Across South Asia, this sense has animated powerful protest movements, some of which could shape their countries’ political trajectories for decades to come.”

The common element of these Gen Z movements was encapsulated at the Oslo conference by María Corina Machado, who was awarded the Peace Prize in 2025 for her role leading the democratic opposition to Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. When society reaches a threshold where conditions have become so dire that more people than not lose the fear of calling things by their name, the aura of authority crumbles, she said. When the reality of people’s lives is so far from the official line, false narratives no longer hold sway.

Following the capture of Maduro by the U.S. military, the installation of an interim government by the Trump administration and the announcement that the U.S. will control 65% of Venezuela’s oil production, Machado insisted that it is now time to open the democratic path and “set an electoral timeline.”

At the Oslo meeting, former Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos, offered some sober advice about the difficult challenges that remain for the long term after signal political victories.

He was awarded the Nobel Prize in 2016 for concluding a peace accord with the Marxist FARC rebels that had gone on for nearly half a century and cost 220,000 lives, with up to 6 million people displaced. Santos was considered a “hawk” as defense minister due to his sometimes-brutal campaigns against the guerrillas. As president, he realized there would never be a military solution to the conflict; it could only be resolved through negotiation and compromise.

Ten years on from that agreement, the peace has generally held as the former guerrillas laid down their arms and participated as a legitimate party in democratic elections. There have also been painful truth and reconciliation processes to hold perpetrators accountable to their victims.

Where the agreement has so far failed is in addressing the root cause of the FARC rebellion in the first place — the poverty and lack of opportunity in those zones of the country where they came to dominate. What has happened instead is that, while the FARC infrastructure was dismantled, the state never stepped in with its own institutions; that void is now filled by the dark civil society of drug and criminal gangs.

Santos’ message to Gen Z: In the wake of any change to the old political system, new institutions that enforce the rule of law, guarantee civic participation and promote economic development must fill the void. Otherwise, it will be back, sooner or later, to square one.

One other thought comes to mind with respect to the social media-driven Gen Z rebellions and revolutions. The connectivity that unites can also divide and disable real transformation.

The internet activist Wael Ghonim was a prominent figure in the so-called Arab Spring’s “Facebook revolution” in Egypt in 2011 that forced President Hosni Mubarak from power. In those early hopeful moments, Ghonim felt the power of connectivity to “speak truth to power.” Yet, when the viral movement shifted from mobilizing angry opposition to constructing a new society, fake news, hate speech, factions and trolls splintered that unity, leaving a vacuum filled by the most organized force left: the Muslim Brotherhood. Their election to power was later overturned by a military coup.

What happened, as Ghonim later put it, is that social media’s participatory capacity to “speak truth to power” transmuted into the opposite challenge: “speaking truth to social media.”

## **Democratic Backsliding**

The dynamics that have mired many nations of the global South in corruption, kleptocracy and autocracy are the same ones that are bringing those conditions to the United States.

> “When the reality of people’s lives is so far from the official line, false narratives no longer hold sway.”

Speaking from her own experience in the Philippines, Maria Ressa sees the deterioration of free expression as the first move in a downward spiral leading to the demise of democracy.

Awarded the Peace Prize in 2021, the defiant journalist has a straightforward formulation: “When truth is stifled, there can be no trust. Without trust there can be no democracy.” So the front-line issue, in both the mature democracies of the U.S. and Europe as well as the global South or Russia, is the battle for the governing narrative.

She breaks the spiral down into three steps:

“First, an administration wages narrative warfare by using governance as a content engine, deliberately fueling conflict to break down a fact-based reality;

“Second, as the shared reality breaks down, democratic institutions that provide checks and balances — like the press and the courts — are systematically delegitimized and dismantled, allowing for the consolidation of executive power;

“Third, with accountability institutions neutralized, the system descends into kleptocracy where state resources are systematically captured and looted to enrich a ruling elite, finance the continuation of the narrative war,” and sustain their grip on power.

While the Gen Z movements are unraveling this spiral in the global South, the mature democracies in the advanced world are just entering it. Indeed, they are on the brink.[](http://www.noemamag.com/the-gen-z-revolt-sweeping-south-asia)

title: Whose AI Will Rule The World?
content:
Credits

Jacob Dreyer is an editor and contributing writer for Noema based in Shanghai.

“_What appears to humanity as the history of capitalism is an invasion from the future by an artificial intelligent space that must assemble itself entirely from its enemy’s resources._“

—Nick Land

SHANGHAI —Today, China and the United States are co-creating a powerful new technology that changes how we think, communicate with each other and understand what consciousness itself means. [Some](https://www.cnbc.com/2018/02/01/google-ceo-sundar-pichai-ai-is-more-important-than-fire-electricity.html) compare it to the invention of fire, or electricity. But a more apt analogy might be the invention of writing: a system that both liberates our thoughts — and constrains them.

When did civilization, as a collective archive of thoughts put down into writing, first begin? Do those beginnings encode certain tendencies into the users of language today, whether those using the language are aware of it or not? Our world has two dominating cultural source codes: one from the West, however construed, and the other that began in Yinxu, Henan, around 3,500 years ago, where the written Chinese language emerged in the form of prophetic oracle bones. Scholars like Yuri Pines have long argued that the ideographic nature of the Chinese script was the primary engine of its cultural continuity.

Take 文, the root word for writing, literature, culture, civilization. The oracle bone inscription was of a person’s body, undergoing a painful ritual transformation of tattooing or scarification. Originally, the word meant “interlocking patterns.” And that is what the Chinese language and civilization form: a huge mental map of interlocking patterns. The written Chinese language is what makes China, China.

Today, the dominant mechanism by which information is transmitted in China is transitioning from the Chinese language to digital networks that communicate in binary or qubits. Paradoxically, this algorithmic form of consciousness is deeply compatible with the traditional Chinese civilizational source code. The concept of an individual being part of a larger network of thought and action transitions seamlessly into the digital age. A civilization whose thinking has always been about the optimized, visual juxtaposition of concepts finds its ultimate realization in the neural network.

## **Language And The Origins Of The Chinese State**

You Shou (1906–1994) was a prominent Chinese archaeologist and master calligrapher. She argued that the oracle bone script (_jiaguwen_) and the bronze inscriptions (_jinwen_) were intrinsically linked to the materials that were used to make them: the bones, the human labor, the metal, the climate. The Chinese characters emerged from the Chinese people and the Chinese landscape; the people and the land predated the words, and the words described and sought to control the people and the land, in a literal sense.

You’s theories linked the development of character stroke structures to the physical tools, labor and materials (bone, bronze, stone) used by ancient peoples: The act of writing was the consummation in and about Yinxu, the place where they were developed, from a hierarchical social structure to the work of the workers who provided the bones and metal in the first place. The evolution of Chinese characters, You wrote, tracks China’s development as a society, with new ways of seeing literally inscribed in the language. Recent examples would be Japanese loan words like _zhuyi_ (主义, “ism”) or _jingji_ (经济, “economy”), or new compound words like _diannao_ (电脑), which means computer. By analyzing character structures, she traced changes in early Chinese geography, social organization and ancient ritual practices. The words, she thought, were invented as a way to answer questions about the order of the cosmos.

The oracle bones were a little like a Ouija board; the person preparing them did not know the outcome in advance. The priest or diviner would pose a question, usually to the high god Di or the ancestors, then apply heat to ox shoulder blades or turtle shells. Shang scribes routinely split a single question for the spirits into positive and negative outcomes: _It will rain tomorrow_ or _It will not rain tomorrow_. Heated, the bone would crack and the holy man would read a response to his question. Auspicious divine answers, dates and consequences would be recorded on the bones. The Shang had intense self-doubt; they couldn’t go to war or plant crops without performing rituals to check in with God. The priests, surrounded as they were by the stench of blood and bone, asked God: What is going to happen to us?

> “And that is what the Chinese language and civilization form: a huge mental map of interlocking patterns. The written Chinese language is what makes China, China.”

And yet, much as the story of Adam and Eve is about forbidden knowledge, the Shang didn’t think of God as telling them these things; what they were doing was more like eavesdropping on divine knowledge. They lived in a world where all of human life was enveloped in the safety of ritual. But by using oracle bones to solve trivial, anxious survival puzzles, they accidentally built the infrastructure of the Chinese mind: assigning an unalterable, concept-driven visual symbol to a natural phenomenon. It was an act of cosmic taming. They were bringing the terrifying, unpredictable movements of ancestors, rivers and seasons into a stable, legible linguistic architecture. Like today’s five-year plans, the oracle bones were not economic forecasts; they were magical, state-directed inscriptions designed to conjure a reality into existence.

These archaic concepts shape the language of Chinese statecraft today. For example, 盟 or alliance, which is used to describe the European Union and ASEAN, consists of a bowl or vessel (皿) at the bottom topped by the character for bright or clear (明), which originally depicted a window illuminated by the moon or by a sacrificial fire. In ancient times, to seal a political pact, lords dug a pit, slaughtered a sacrificial animal (often a bull or dog), cut off its left ear and caught the blood in a bronze vessel (皿). The lords smeared raw blood on their lips and swore an oath to the gods (明). The 盟 character thus physically encodes the wet, copper flavor of shared blood that bound ancient factions together.

Yinxu was, some say, a city of perhaps 150,000 people, and had no physical walls but was sharply divided by class. The Shang elite lived in a state of ritualistic intoxication. Occupying grand palaces, they spent their days hunting big game on the Henan plains (elephants, rhinoceroses and tigers still roamed the warm, humid landscape); drinking vast quantities of warm, herb-infused wine from heavy bronze _jue_ vessels; and conducting military raids on neighboring tribes. Their entire psychological reality was geared toward validating their lineage through conspicuous feasting and violence.

Shang craftsmen, meanwhile, enjoyed a privileged, middle-tier status, protected by the state because they produced the technology of power. In industrial quarters like Xiaomintun, they operated massive, hyper-coordinated bronze foundries. The vast majority of the population were ordinary peasants whose lives were grindingly hard. They did not live in houses; they lived in pits dug into the earth and covered by rough timber and thatch roofs to shield them from the freezing winters.

Aside from bronze, Yinxu’s largest industry was bone tool production. In a single workshop site, archaeologists uncovered millions of discarded animal bones (primarily cattle, pig and deer) that had been systematically carved into arrows, hairpins and awls. The city must have smelled of boiled animal fat, charcoal smoke and raw marrow. When a king died, or when a major palace foundation was laid, hundreds of human beings were systematically executed to serve as structural or spiritual filler. Captured prisoners were bound, decapitated or dismembered by the dozens, their heads buried in neat, geometric rows in the palace plazas to appease the high god Di and the royal ancestors. To keep the world from collapsing, the Shang kings had to unleash torrents of human blood, torch bones with fire and mobilize hundreds of thousands of hands to dig earth and melt bronze.

> “A civilization whose thinking has always been about the optimized, visual juxtaposition of concepts finds its ultimate realization in the neural network.”

I first learned of You Shou while researching the history of the Cultural Revolution in Harbin. She was at the center of a group called the “eight weirdos,” Harbin scholars who were singled out for torment by Red Guards who were trying to eradicate the “four olds,” (四旧): old ideas, old culture, old customs and old habits. The Communist project had to crush scholars like You Shou because her work revealed that the Party was not a radical break from the past, but an unwitting captive of it. The uncanny image of a hierarchical and violent Chinese elite who used semi-mystical techniques to conjure a future into being was too uncomfortable, heresy to the notion of a New China.

None of the great ethicists of ancient Chinese culture — Confucius, Laozi and friends — lived in Yinxu. All of that came later. But the invention of language was a prerequisite to their work.

The conclusion might be that today, as the world stumbles terrified into future climate change and cultural decadence, that sometimes, the sacrifices work. The AI being built is not a good in itself; the questions we ask it may be as trivial as the Shang asking the oracle bones what part of the forest was a good place to hunt. But the platform created may birth systems, ideas and thoughts which we cannot currently imagine, in formats that exceed our wildest dreams. That’s what happened to the Shang, anyway.

## **The Scientific Sovereign**

For the past few months, I’ve been corresponding with [Pan Jianwei](https://www.technologyreview.com/2018/12/19/1571/the-man-turning-china-into-a-quantum-superpower/), China’s quantum computing champion, trying to understand his views on how Chinese science fits into the world and what the significance of quantum computing will be for China’s future. Pan’s adviser, Anton Zeilinger, won the Nobel Prize in physics in 2022. Working in Zeilinger’s lab, Pan was part of the elite team that achieved the world’s first experimental demonstration of quantum teleportation in 1997. When Zeilinger asked Pan what his long-term dream was, Pan famously replied: “To build a world-class quantum physics lab in China.” By 2016, Pan had become the mastermind behind Micius, a satellite that enables quantum communication across vast distances. Pan is largely seen as one of China’s most likely candidates for the Nobel. But China has bigger fish to fry.

Quantum computing replaces the traditional language by which computers organize information with a new way, our understanding of which originated with Albert Einstein’s theories. While classical computers rely on binary logic — processing information through rigid transistors as individual bits that must be strictly a 0 or a 1 — quantum computing uses qubits. Qubits are particles that exist based on two seemingly contradictory concepts: superposition and entanglement. Superposition means a qubit can exist in multiple states simultaneously — a complex, fluid blend of both 0 and 1 at the same time. Entanglement is a unique connection where qubits become linked, allowing a change in one to instantly dictate the state of another.

By manipulating these fluid probabilities rather than processing data step by step, a quantum computer can map out massive, complex solution spaces all at once. In this sense, quantum computing is to computing what Chinese characters are to the Roman alphabet: Both apparently fulfill the same function, but the way in which they do so is radically different.

> “AI may birth systems, ideas and thoughts which we cannot currently imagine, in formats that exceed our wildest dreams. That’s what happened to the Shang, anyway.”

In recent months, the White House has been [tweeting](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/06/ushering-in-the-next-frontier-of-quantum-innovation/) about quantum supremacy alongside the usual half-baked [AI-generated images](https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/qanon-memes-trump-quantum/); in the [2025 National Security Strategy](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025-National-Security-Strategy.pdf), quantum is mentioned, along with AI and biotech, as a field that the U.S. must not cede to rivals like China. It’s seen as important because if China breaks through on quantum computing, it’ll have a way around traditional public-key encryption and be able to read all of America’s secrets.

Although he is increasingly prominent in China’s political ecosystem, Pan is not a member of the Communist Party. His allegiance lies with the Jiusan Society, one of China’s eight legally sanctioned political parties. Rather than being elevated to an administrative role like, for example, Chen Jining, the environmental scientist turned Shanghai party secretary, Pan continues to manage his quantum lab in Hefei. In a China increasingly more interested in social development through advanced computation rather than human resources, that position might be equally powerful — and a lot more fun. Instead of wasting time navigating the standard, hyper-competitive and granular grant application cycles that consume Western researchers, Pan just gets large sums of money transferred into his jurisdiction. Under Xi Jinping’s mandate for absolute “sci-tech self-reliance,” Pan’s operational authority means that if he identifies a critical bottleneck, the state quickly funnels funding and manpower directly to him.

His work and influence extend far beyond university walls to the commercial monetization of his discoveries. QuantumCTek was founded by his academic research team, for example. In a massive vote of confidence, China Telecom acquired a 23% stake in the firm to build out unhackable national communications infrastructure based directly on Pan’s proprietary hardware. In this sense, Pan exemplifies a new class in China: politically untouchable, trusted enough to receive a blank check for funding and proactively supported in commercialization by state-owned entities.

In an email to me, Pan shared five pages of thoughts of his own and other quantum scientists in China. In short, he said, China’s government believes that technological change creates economic change creates political change. It also believes that the world is on the brink of a technological revolution driven by AI, quantum computing, biotech, new energy sources, materials science and other fields. In the tradition of the Shang, the Chinese are ready to make any sacrifice, as long as the new language that is being created is one they understand.

As Hong Ding, a Chinese Academy of Sciences academician, put it in an email to me:

Basic science … expands, revises or deepens our understanding of the laws and mechanisms themselves. It asks a question whose answer we genuinely do not know, and — this is the part that never stops surprising me — the answer, pursued for its own sake, later reshapes the world.

## **A New Golden Age?**

Michael Kratsios is an alumnus of arguably the two most forward-looking incubators of science policy in the world today: Thiel Capital and Tsinghua University. Today, he is Trump’s science adviser. In his [report](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Science-A-New-Golden-Age.pdf) on reforming American science, which he presents as being the biggest revision to American science policy since Vannevar Bush’s postwar “Science: The Endless Frontier,” we see one of the most concrete and detailed indications yet that the Trump administration is adopting Chinese mechanisms, inspired by a close and meticulous study of what makes the Chinese model successful.

Kratsios likely wouldn’t admit it, but his report represents a fundamental shift away from the traditional, decentralized Western model of free academic inquiry toward a centralized, mission-driven, state-backed system that mirrors Beijing’s tech-governance model. For example, echoing a long-time Thiel idea, the report fiercely critiques traditional, consensus-driven Western academic peer-review boards as sluggish and conservative; by definition, peer review means that new ideas must be checked by the gatekeepers of the old. Kratsios proposes a “broader menu of selection mechanisms,” specifically introducing “golden tickets” that empower individual, state-appointed reviewers to unilaterally fund highly ambitious, high-risk proposals without consensus approval. That’s exactly what high-flyer scientists like Pan Jianwei have: They’ve earned the trust of the system and are treated as partners in a venture capital fund.

The centerpieces of the Kratsios report are the “Genesis Mission” and a newly funded National Science Foundation initiative called “X-Labs.” These are explicitly structured as “Manhattan Project-style” efforts designed to build highly focused, multidisciplinary independent research organizations that apply AI directly to accelerated scientific productivity, totally bypassing legacy academic boundaries. Kratsios is effectively recreating the structure of China’s National Laboratories and State Key Laboratories (such as Pan Jianwei’s quantum facilities in Hefei or Fudan University’s Xuemin Institute, itself modeled on the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton).

But even if the U.S. adopts many Chinese methods, it lacks the critical ingredient of Chinese science success: Chinese people. Lots of them. Effectively, Kratsios is proposing to make up for this gap by letting AI, a “country of geniuses in a datacenter” as Dario Amodei once put it, do for America what millions of Chinese STEM graduates do for China.

Democratic critics (like Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California) have explicitly denounced this policy, noting that the administration “has been systematically destroying the U.S. science enterprise.” Dan Wang and Julian Gewirtz [criticized](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/28/opinion/ai-race-china-us.html) Trump policies in The New York Times for emulating China, particularly the proactive way that the Pentagon is seeking to supervise Anthropic, which they allege is a direct copy of China’s state capitalism.

> “In the tradition of the Shang, the Chinese are ready to make any sacrifice, as long as the new language that is being created is one they understand.”

Beijing doesn’t nationalize tech firms; it integrates the state into private enterprises. But to be fair to Kratsios, China’s science structure is clearly working, and the degree of integration between policymakers, fundamental research (in fields like materials science or chemistry), burgeoning fields (like batteries) and global domination of supply chains, can feel new. The Thiel wing of the Trump administration is seeking truth from facts. The questions for Americans are: Is the overall strategy of rivaling Chinese scale effects via AI likely to work? And: As we pursue these processes, how will our own society change? Are we comfortable with that?

In 2014, Thiel wrote in his tech-founder bible “Zero to One” that China is a society characterized by definite pessimism: The Chinese believe that tragic disaster lurks, so they make comprehensive plans to avoid it. In contrast, American society of the Vannevar Bush era (the 1950s) was one of definite optimism: America made plans because it believed that the future was bright. These outlooks don’t neatly map onto countries today (if they ever did), but if anything, as AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans.

The Silicon Valley radicals adjacent to Thiel — and therefore the White House — have been making provocative remarks about science for some time. For example, Curtis Yarvin recently [asserted](https://x.com/curtis_yarvin/status/2084675074221912452) that NASA was founded by Nazis who’d gone to Alabama. Yarvin’s claim rests entirely on the historical reality of Operation Paperclip, the American mission to relocate top German scientists and engineers to the U.S. during the final stages of World War II. China today resembles the U.S. then: an industrial superpower that senses it is not quite as sophisticated as the decadent power it wishes to replace. From this vantage point, Kratsios (a former instructor at Tsinghua who knows what the Chinese are thinking as well as any American government official) doesn’t want the U.S. to be eclipsed.

The Chinese AI policy that American policymakers like Kratsios are inspired by proceeds with great clarity: There is a list of problems and AI is being used systematically to solve those problems. The Chinese assume that private companies and new technologies that depend on government support and the participation and consent of the population should serve that population. And as with the rest of their products, what happens in China doesn’t stay in China, but is exported to whoever will take it, which increasingly means the Global South.

## **When AI Runs The World**

Not long ago, I was invited to Nanning, the capital of Guangxi Province, a three-hour train ride from Shenzhen but culturally a backwater.[](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/baike.baidu.com/en/item/China-ASEAN*20Artificial*20Intelligence*20Application*20Cooperation*20Center/943335__;JSUlJSU!!NLFGqXoFfo8MMQ!uO5nyshq6xRpbTq5fbxHNq9PGd8yUBtc3QB2YRz1XTbTehTd4rWmnMT9Yr7Ml6vjwQOmLR-ROHKe4ePEomrDy2cc7rSyqgMIvFYT$)The Chinese five-year plans allocate different tasks to different regions: Big cities like Beijing and Shanghai are for capital-heavy innovation and research, which Guangxi is positioned to disseminate to Southeast Asia. Inside the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center, a digital display advertised different AI applications: agriculture, logistics, public safety, manufacturing, local finance, healthcare and education. China invites leaders from Vietnam, Laos and Indonesia to this place and says: _Look, we figured out how to use AI to make our farmers richer, our factories better, our streets safer. We can do that for you too._

Nanning itself felt like a display of what Chinese style development could bring. Technically, this is the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with ethnic minorities such as the Zhuang dominating. Signs on government buildings are bilingual. Nanning’s nominal GDP per capita sits at nearly $10,000, double Vietnam’s and nearly five times higher than in Laos or Cambodia. And the infrastructure, public safety and general atmosphere is excellent. So the vibe of the AI center was very much showing off: _All this could be yours. Sign on the dotted line._

The Chinese government’s AI+ plan focuses on applications in sectors that the government has a role in and often in places where the population can’t afford what others can (high-quality education, healthcare, etc.). AI is understood as a tool, or perhaps a commodity like electricity, and the Chinese plan is to use that tool to solve Chinese problems — [reducing](https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-economy/article/3355153/china-plans-embed-ai-energy-infrastructure-optimise-power-grid-efficiency) the cost of electricity, [safeguarding](http://english.scio.gov.cn/chinavoices/2025-03/24/content_117782255.html) the country’s food supply, [providing](https://healthpolicy-watch.news/china-long-term-care-ai/) national healthcare via AI-driven medical solutions. China’s civilization, patriarchal and authoritarian though it may be, has a clear goal in mind: make Chinese people safer, richer, stronger and, ultimately, more Chinese.

> “AI is understood as a tool, or perhaps a commodity like electricity, and the Chinese plan is to use that tool to solve Chinese problems.”

At the recent World AI Conference in Shanghai, I saw an ancient Chinese scroll painting underneath a fancy screen made by [CamScanner](https://www.camscanner.com/). The proximity of the pair seemed to underline the message that Chinese tech companies are expected to serve Chinese civilizational needs — as defined by the government. Even when this feels like an afterthought, it’s politically important for Chinese AI companies to symbolically pledge allegiance to their country’s heritage.

That’s them; American civilization is different. Many aspects of the Chinese model would not fly in America. Surveillance, for example. Look at the backlash to Flock. A government that makes decisions for individuals without asking for their permission is, generally, an unwelcome idea in the States.

But Americans need not adopt any of China’s specific solutions to ask the important questions: What is AI actually doing for Americans? Is the general population in control, or are the Silicon Valley oligarchs? And which system —China’s state-directed planning or America’s obviously eroded democratic capitalism — will be more universally acceptable over the long term?

title: A New Kind Of Creative Poverty
content:
Credits

Afra Wang is a California-based writer and journalist who focuses on technological modernity through a humanistic lens, spanning China and Silicon Valley in the global AI age. She writes concurrent.blog and is a frequent contributor to many outlets.

_**Editor’s Note:**Noema is transparent about AI use in its pieces. We publish original human-generated ideas but allow authorized, disclosed use of AI in certain cases. Please see details at the end of this piece._

During a dark stretch of Covid, I dove into Joan Didion’s _“_ The Year of Magical Thinking,” her book about processing her husband’s death. Didion wrote that she could not give away his shoes. She had managed the suits, the shirts, the jackets. But when she got to the shoes, she paused: “I stood there for a moment, then realized why: he would need shoes if he was to return.”

I was living in solitude in an apartment recently emptied by a long-term relationship. When the rental lease lapsed, I renewed it and renewed it again, keeping the furniture exactly as it had been, the lamp at the same angle. What Didion was dealing with was, in [Orwell’s words](https://www.telelib.com/authors/O/OrwellGeorge/essay/insidewhale_1.html), “the recognizable experiences of human beings.” Through her writing, I felt relief wash over me as I suddenly saw my own stalled life right under my nose.

What many readers come to Didion for — what I went to her for — is the record of a mind at work on its own chaos, a way of processing thought, of handling the formless weather in the head. I love watching her spill it all out, like discovering the neighbors’ house is total chaos, and feeling assured that no one’s life is truly put-together.

Being gripped by the experiences evoked by writers like Didion could be a survival trait, shaped over countless years of evolution. The psychologist Bruce Hood [argues](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/188116/the-domesticated-brain-by-hood-bruce/9780141974873) that we are a self-domesticated species: Over roughly a thousand generations, human beings have favored cooperation and sociability as traits in our mates and allies. In doing so, we rewired our brains to read, track, mimic and crave other minds. We have been self-domesticating, Hood writes, “through the invention of culture and practices that ensure that we can live together,” and eventually win the evolution game. To be gripped by another person’s inner life is old equipment built into us.

Social media is a product of this ancient urge, a machine for exercising our interest in other humans at a scale evolution never planned for. But what happens when we learn that this other human, or this “recognizable experience,” has been artificially generated by an LLM? Maybe this is why the counterfeit cuts the way it does. AI slop feels like betrayal. There is this haunting feeling when you lean toward a face and then find only a mask, with no person behind it.

And this feeling is probably one reason people have become obsessed with running the words they read through Pangram, a tool to detect AI writing, or other such detectors. Almost every writer I know has some visceral repulsion at the tells — “tapestry,” “crystallize,” “delve,” or “it’s not X, it’s Y” — that low-effort, overfitted register. Probably no one online reacts more violently than the British writer Sam Kriss, in an [essay](https://samkriss.substack.com/p/if-you-let-ai-do-your-writing-i-will) titled “If you let AI do your writing, I will come to your house and kill you”:

I hate it. I find it viscerally disgusting; a cold shudder like someone’s poured jelly down the back of my neck. I hate that it’s everywhere; I hate that when I read basically anything now I’m constantly on alert, twitching like a schizo in an underpass. Is this thing really what it says it is? Is this person actually a robot in disguise? Nice little personal essay you’ve got there, lady, but I know what you really are; time to get my knife out, time to start digging around under your skin until I find the wires.

This urge — when a sentence feels off, and you must dig beneath its skin to find the wires — might be familiar to you. At a [conference](https://manifest.is/) not long ago, I watched Chris Best, Substack’s chief executive, and Oliver Habryka, who runs the [rationalist forum LessWrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/users/habryka4), discuss this disturbance. Both platforms, in their early days, were built on the assumption that a reader can trust the writing in front of them to be authentic and human (and distinctive from institutional writing). Today, that assumption no longer holds.

LessWrong now requires its writers to disclose when they have used AI. As of publication, Substack has also recently [launched a feature](https://post.substack.com/p/against-claudefishing) using Pangram-style detection to reduce “Claudefishing,” so readers don’t “unwittingly invest their attention in something with no human thought on the other end.” Everyone seems exhausted by the constant tax of suspecting AI behind every sentence. The tech industry’s actions and inaction (LinkedIn, for instance, has become a dumpster of AI slop people laugh at) reflect a growing backlash against soulless slop.

> “AI slop feels like betrayal.”

I, too, have struggled with anger over sloppy AI writing that has made me viscerally uncomfortable. My reactions can be a little pathological: I fanatically delete my own em dashes, and I once even mistakenly thought a few sentences a writer friend wrote were AI-generated. But I also must confess to my own relationship with AI: Because English is my second language, I rely heavily on Claude as a grammar checker— to smooth the bumps in my sentences and remove the ESL flavor. I used to have a somewhat cringy analogy to describe writing in English: installing a pair of mechanical wings. These wings carry me to vast terrains and audiences I couldn’t reach before, even though they sometimes feel artificial. AI makes those wings less heavy, but more not-entirely-me. So when I do get angry at AI writing, I also try to understand where the anger comes from —and then I wonder how angry I am allowed to be.

## **Escaping The Simplified Chinese Internet**

For a long time, I felt trapped in my mother tongue after I left China at the age of 17. More precisely, I mean a particular kind of language born out of China’s enclosed internet. It is a strange language that sticks with you — long since severed from the depth and philosophical richness of Chinese — tamed and flattened by years of shrinking space for discussion and infested with algorithm-favored brevity.

Out of self-mockery and sympathy, people coined a term, the “Simplified Chinese Internet” (简中互联网). It is a phrase that immediately suggests crippled thoughts, one-dimensional topics, evasively coded slang that dodges censorship yet means nothing, alongside advanced infrastructure and intense scrutiny. It was the Simplified Chinese internet itself that I wanted to escape. And the language used on it can be understood as the product of a long reward-and-punishment environment that resembles today’s LLM training. Over time, even the most creative and rebellious minds are tamed and overfitted, until they can only produce “acceptable” continuations — for public “safety.” Of course, precisely because the “Simplified Chinese Internet” is constrained and censored, it can sometimes inspire strange, ingenious ways of expressing discontent. The 2022 “White Paper” protests are a perfect example: Demonstrators opposed Zero-COVID by holding up blank sheets of paper, because the state (and the algorithms) can’t censor emptiness. But such cleverness is not a credit to censorship itself, or evidence that authoritarian control doesn’t suffocate creativity and self-expression. That conclusion would be utterly wrong. In reality, most of those who are “unsafe” simply left the “Simplified Chinese Internet” long ago or became idle.

That kind of creative poverty makes me think about LLMs’ inability to be original writers. In the past couple of months, many people using LLMs to write stories have noticed a [strange effect](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.26492v1): a disproportionate number of stories about lighthouses, clockmakers and librarians — and these stories would always feature a protagonist named “Elias Thorne.” Elias’s name now turns up everywhere: on self-published Amazon books, fake news sites and YouTube videos. It’s a typical phenomenon of model collapse — a failure state where a model produces repetitive, low-diversity outputs. One unverified guess is that alignment makes LLMs prefer the “safest” options during post-training, which steers them from saying things that are low-reward (inappropriate content, copyright infringement, etc.). An LLM will avoid every possible minefield and choose outputs that maximize the reward within its system parameters, so we’ll end up with a story about a lonely Elias Thorne living in a lighthouse at the edge of the world. It’s almost like asking an 18-year-old Chinese student to tell a story on a test: the result is a cookie-cutter lineup of Lu Xun, Helen Keller, Madame Curie, Qian Xuesen and Du Fu — morality-driven, legible packages that reliably earn a good [Gaokao score](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/features/understanding-the-gaokao-exam).

But we wicked human beings, especially in creative fields, are very good at working against all of the above. As writer [Celine Nguyen said](https://open.substack.com/pub/personalcanon/p/good-artists-copy-ai-artists-____?r=1bqgb&selection=85be3b68-5b71-4397-b1ef-78e3f2aedc31&utm_campaign=post-share-selection&utm_medium=web&aspectRatio=instagram&textColor=%23ffffff&bgImage=true), “the core obligation of the artwork is to move me, not to make itself legible to me.” What great writing might never come to be in a reward-and-punishment regime solely intent on maximizing the score? I learned the answer to that, oddly enough, in childhood with the 19th-century French poet Baudelaire.

I am still amused and haunted by that accidental childhood encounter with his Gothic and sinful poems on death, hell, sex and decay in “Les Fleurs du mal,” or “The Flowers of Evil.”

> “Precisely because the ‘Simplified Chinese Internet’ is constrained and censored, it can sometimes inspire strange, ingenious ways of expressing discontent.”

I was probably 8 or 9, reaching up to the lower shelf of my father’s bookcase in our home in Taiyuan, in northern China, looking for something less childish to read. The cover had convinced me the book was about some Greek heroes and European adventures. It was a small, old book, brittle-paged, translated by scholar Guo Hong’an. My father, who I suspect never read Baudelaire closely himself, only told me the poet was a great man. “A Western master, like Shakespeare, Dickens, Victor Hugo. A classic!” He said it with reverence, and with the delight of a father whose daughter had reached for the West so young.

“Quote his lines in your homework essays next week _,_”my father suggested _._ And so, without warning, I walked into Baudelaire’s imagination before I knew what “Western master” meant, and the most intrusive, alienating passages imprinted themselves on me — in a Chinese translation that was both beautiful and terrifying.

My father — a trend-chasing magazine editor in northern China, longing for America and liberalism — had bought the book in his early 20s, during one of PRC’s rather open, pluralistic stretches, when the country allowed itself to discuss Baudelaire in daylight. Through the Cultural Revolution, when the only safe-to-read book was Mao’s “Little Red Book,” the literary establishment took its cue from Soviet doctrine and [filed](https://www.mycaijing.com/article/detail/193029?source_id=40) Baudelaire’s writings under the decadence of late, rotting capitalism; to read him was heresy, a “poison” of degeneracy.

And yet he survived, passed hand to hand in secret by underground readers in Beijing, Shanghai, even in the steep mountains of Chongqing. Bei Dao, an iconoclastic poet my father once admired, has written about what those smuggled poems meant in the dark times: We scavenged together for Baudelaire’s scattered poems, as if looking for a needle in the sea, and copied them down carefully and neatly into notebooks. For the Beijing underground literary world, such samizdat was a kind of spiritual guide.

Many years later, now living in California, I can still describe that childhood afternoon in China with _“_ Les Fleurs du mal” as a terrifying, exciting, gut-wrenching ride. Those poems are about blood-sucking [vampires](https://fleursdumal.org/poem/128) and sexual desire and rotting corpses and a seductive woman decaying into a gruesome pile of bones by the roadside. They were nothing like the Chinese children’s books, nothing like my textbooks, nothing like any Western classic I’d been handed. I knew enough to understand I was reading something forbidden, something that had slipped through a crack and that my father would probably take it back the moment he realized what it was.

I never did take my father’s advice and quote Baudelaire in my homework. It took me a while to scrub the shock and the shame of reading him out of my head. His deeper hold surfaced only in adulthood, and only years later. Only once I had read more widely did I understand what he actually was. All that moral trespass, he had poured into the strictest inherited forms of French verse (the alexandrine, the quatrain, the sonnet). Inside those orderly meters the reader does not find the themes the form trains you to expect. Shock _is_ the point.

Baudelaire was prosecuted the instant “Les Fleurs du mal” appeared, in the summer of 1857 — charged by French authorities with both blasphemy and what the court called an outrage to public decency; he was convicted for indecency, and six of his poems were ordered removed from the book. Condemned in Paris; then, a century on, condemned again by Maoist orthodoxy as bourgeois rot. He resurfaced in the loosening China of the 1980s and ’90s and was collected by hungry liberal young men like my father, who mistook the most subversive 19th-century book in our house for Western canon.

Strangely, AI is what recently sent me back to Baudelaire. Against all that balanced, polished and polite prose written by machines using a mixture of statistical centrality and learning from human feedback scores, I found myself missing Baudelaire — missing the bookshelf, the second one down, which stayed faintly sinful for years. Baudelaire spiritually represents the edge cases the LLMs are trained against.

## **Good Taste?**

My friend Jerry Zhou, who worked on LLM training at Microsoft AI, told me a model is like a single person, and millions of people around the world are all asking that one person questions. If the questions are similar, the answers converge. And unless you intervene at the level of the LLM weights or training objective, you should never expect this person to surprise you, and especially not shock you.

> “Baudelaire spiritually represents the edge cases the LLMs are trained against.”

Claude’s own “[Constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution),” a document some 80 pages long that teaches the model how to behave, instructs it to be “genuinely good, wise, and virtuous”: to be tactful, helpful, graceful, honest and, above all, to “help people in the way a good person would.” And I wonder whether today’s Baudelaire archetypes, those writers and artists out there, would ever want to create what a “good person” would create. To many, I suspect the phrase itself might insult their craft or be stultifying.

I keep returning to a line from Simon Schama’s “The Power of Art.” It is the book’s first sentence: “great art has dreadful manners.” Schama, a historian at Columbia University, tells us that art is a “thug,” “merciless and wily.” It will “grab you in a headlock, rough up your composure, and then proceed in short order to re-arrange your sense of reality.”

I admit it is unfair to expect every writer and artist to be as provocative as Baudelaire. But that episode from my childhood formed an early conviction: that greatness can arrive in the margins, be deemed unsafe and still elude any empirical measure. That a “Western master” need not be a Dickens or a [Hugo](https://archive-yaleglobal.yale.edu/content/victor-hugos-chinese-adventures), one of those virtuous authors who “care for the proletariat and the downtrodden,” as PRC curriculum prefers. He can just as well be a man condemned, across more than a century, by the French courts and Maoism alike.

That afternoon, after I slid Baudelaire back onto the shelf, I went to my desk and finished my homework. In the years after, I must have written countless essays, all of them obedient to the specifications of the Chinese education system, perfectly legible to my teachers. Neither they nor I would remember a single one. Even now I am still trying to unlearn the muscle memory those schools and the Simplified Chinese internet drilled into me.

Posterity’s verdict on Baudelaire is that he is the last poet of French classicism and the first of French modernism. That evil book would, many years on, make him the father of French Symbolism. Nearly 100 years later, on May 31, 1949, the judgment against him was formally overturned, and the six banned poems were returned to print in France. The great 20th-century critic Walter Benjamin [called](https://dokumen.pub/walter-benjamin-and-the-arcades-project-9781472547842-9780826463869-9780826463876.html) him the forerunner of the modern poet, locked in a life-or-death struggle with the urban commodity capitalism then rising in an industrializing Paris — one that no one yet knew how to describe. In an old France without Baudelaire, no one had the language for the new urban reality that modernity had produced. Baudelaire, however, displayed what Benjamin [described](https://dokumen.pub/walter-benjamin-and-the-arcades-project-9781472547842-9780826463869-9780826463876.html) as the “shocking, raw immediacy of his sense impressions” of that reality, which is full of sensations of modernity like prostitutes, mud, gaslight, jostling crowds and perpetual alienation.

In a mercantile Paris, who needed what Benjamin [called](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/4550655) “a ragpicker who gathers up the city’s detritus only to turn it into poetry”? Who could have imagined that this ragpicker would become a representative figure of modernity’s decay? The blind spot the researcher Zhengdong Wang names in judging what an LLM can do, in an essay on[AI evaluation](https://zhengdongwang.com/2024/12/29/2024-letter.html), is a blind spot in human society too: “We don’t even know what we really want until we see it, at which point it may change.” _Yes, the world didn’t know it wanted a Baudelaire, for a long time, until it understood him_. The old coordinates, like the French state that prosecuted Baudelaire and took his 50 francs, can neither permit nor comprehend an experience that is invisible and wholly real. This, I think, is the very sensation my father’s generation went looking for, those Chinese who came of age in the Cultural Revolution. Baudelaire had leaped clear of every measure his society used to sort “good” from “bad”, and was punished for the leap. Bei Dao, the poet who kept Baudelaire as a secret spiritual icon through those years, went on with his peers, in the more open China of the 1980s, to found the[Misty Poetry movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misty_Poets) that deeply influenced my father. The movement was set against almost everything the Cultural Revolution’s benchmarks had prized—those socialist-realist works and political lyric poems marked by positive emotion, educational value, with the author cast as a representative of “the people” or “the era”—and instead was filled with the unknowable and the unforeseen.

> “The awkward truth is AI still gives us flattened prose and bad writing.”

Today’s Silicon Valley somewhat resembles the French state that punished Baudelaire, an age intoxicated by abundance and by its own industrial revolution. We are being persuaded that AI will hand us prosperity and an intelligence explosion, that it will cure cancer any day now. The researchers working on [recursive self-improvement](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/recursive-self-improvement) have convinced me that AI will excel at every benchmark we can put into words. And yet the awkward truth is AI still gives us flattened prose and bad writing.

AI feels disenchanted; it didn’t “revolutionize” content. It’s increasingly “[same-ifying](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-00781-9)” writing, design, and everything related to human expression, and shaping our thoughts in reverse. Over the last few years, many in Silicon Valley have held up “taste” as an antidote. People argue that “good taste” makes one’s eye discerning and can identify ineffable qualities that stand out in the ocean of infinite content generated by AI. For leaders, “taste is a competitive advantage,” an article in The Atlantic [claims](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2025/06/good-taste-ai/683101/). Culture critic and software designer Celine Nguyen [observed](https://asteriskmag.com/issues/15/why-we-like-things) that “taste has become the catch-all term,” and Kyle Chayka, a staff writer at The New Yorker, [suggested](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/infinite-scroll/why-tech-bros-are-now-obsessed-with-taste) it has become the latest Silicon Valley cliché — like “disruption” was in the 2010s. The word has hardened into something widely repeated and inherently profitable, a lever for correcting what AI produces. [Taste is the new moat](https://wangcong.org/2026-01-13-personal-taste-is-the-moat.html), these AI entrepreneurs say.

The term has also traveled to China and its equally pervasive AI industry. On the Simplified Chinese internet, the tech junkies and AI practitioners trade notes on how to build things with “good taste.” My internal seismograph reads otherwise. Some of this “good taste” will soon become the new mid-curve of mediocrity, the new predictability, the new “it’s not X, it’s Y.” Baudelaire would have no use for it. He was a man who deliberately set out to provoke revulsion. He believed “the mixture of the grotesque and the tragic is as pleasing to the mind as dissonances to blasé ears.” A man proud of his bad taste. “What is exhilarating in bad taste,” he wrote in [his private journals](https://blacksunlit.com/2017/07/excerpts-from-my-heart-laid-bare-by-charles-baudelaire-translated-from-french-by-rainer-j-hanshe/), “is the aristocratic pleasure of giving offense.”
